# Bootstrapping experiments {#sec-bootstrapping}

The question of this book is whether word–object mapping can be **bootstrapped** from
naturalistic data — whether a learner can climb from naive contrastive training toward the
ceiling using only signal it could plausibly have. This chapter maps that climb with a single,
systematic design: train on **all** of BabyView (36 children, 911k pairs on an 80% video split),
evaluate on the out-of-sample **Konkle** benchmark (@sec-eval), and measure what each mechanism
contributes against oracle toplines. Everything is 3 seeds; the primary number is Konkle test-60.

## Three bootstraps

Every mechanism here is a form of *self-supervised selection* — deciding what to attend to
without being told the answer — at a different grain (@sec-mechanisms):

- **Region** (MIL max over frame cells): *where* in the frame is the referent.
- **Frame** (MIL max over a ±2 s window): *which moment* shows it best.
- **Utterance** (EM reweighting of pairs by self-estimated alignment): *which pairs* are aligned.

The oracles that bound them come from the Gemini annotation of @sec-data: **alignment** (which
pairs are truly referential) and the **referent label** (which word names the object).

## The ladder

![The bootstrapping ladder. Green rungs are **free** — achievable with no labels; blue rungs are
**oracles** — upper bounds that require alignment or referent labels we do not have at training
time. Bars show absolute achieved accuracy per condition; the oracle rungs are each measured from
the region-MIL baseline (they are alternative branches, not stacked on frame-MIL). Perfect labels
cannot exceed ~81 on these frozen features.](figures/fig_waterfall_ladder.png){#fig-ladder width=95%}

| Rung | Konkle | Δ | kind |
|---|---|---|---|
| chance | 25 | — | — |
| pure learning (whole-frame, noisy data) | 52.9 ± 1.7 | +27.9 | free |
| **+ region MIL** | 62.6 ± 1.7 | **+9.7** | free |
| **+ frame MIL** | 65.0 ± 1.8 | **+2.4** | free |
| + alignment filter | 68.5 ± 1.3 | +5.9 | oracle |
| + word selection | 73.2 ± 1.2 | +4.7 | oracle |
| + vision-binding | 81.3 ± 2.6 | +8.1 | oracle |
| ceiling | ~81 | — | +18.7 unlearnable from these features |

Two facts frame everything. **The free gains are large and get you most of the way:** pure
contrastive learning on noisy data already reaches 52.9, region MIL adds +9.7, and frame MIL a
further +2.4, landing an **unaided** learner at **65.0**. Above that, every rung is an **oracle** —
it needs information (which pairs are aligned; which word is the referent) we cannot access at
training time. **No self-supervised mechanism we tried climbs those oracle rungs.**

## What the bootstraps buy

![The three self-supervised bootstraps. Region and frame selection are real, free gains; the
utterance EM bootstrap is null within seed noise.](figures/fig_waterfall_mechanisms.png){#fig-mechanisms width=80%}

**Region MIL (+9.7)** is the single largest free gain. Scoring the utterance against the
best-matching cell of a frame — with no detector and no labels — does implicit referent
*localization*, and it lands the unaided learner most of the way to the oracle filter on its own.

**Frame MIL (+2.4)** is a modest but consistent free gain. A region × frame $2\times2$ isolates it:

| | single frame | + frame MIL (±2 s) |
|---|---|---|
| whole-frame | 52.9 ± 1.7 | 55.5 ± 1.7 (+2.6) |
| region | 62.6 ± 1.7 | **65.0 ± 1.8 (+2.4)** |

Selecting the best *moment* in a short window adds ~+2.4 on top of region selection (positive in
all three seeds), roughly additive with region's +9.7. Which-moment matters, a little, on top of
which-region.

### How wide should the window be?

Frame MIL has one free parameter — how much time around the utterance the learner is allowed to
look over. Widening it trades off two things: a longer window is more likely to *contain* the
referential moment, but it also dilutes the selection with more off-target frames. We can just
measure it, holding region MIL fixed and stretching the window from a single frame to ±2 s to ±5 s
(at 1 fps, 5 and 11 candidate frames):

| window | candidate frames | Konkle test-60 (3 seeds) | Δ vs. prev |
|---|---|---|---|
| single frame | 1 | 62.6 ± 1.7 | — |
| ±2 s | 5 | 65.0 ± 1.8 | +2.4 |
| ±5 s | 11 | **66.8 ± 0.6** | +1.8 |

The gain is **monotone with diminishing returns**: each widening still helps, by a little less. At
±5 s the containment benefit is still winning over the dilution cost — the referential moment is
often just outside a ±2 s window, and letting the max reach for it recovers another ~+1.8. But the
curve is clearly bending, and ±5 s is already 11 frames of a 1 fps stream; there is no regime change
waiting at a wider window, only a slow approach to whatever the region-MIL selection can extract.
We keep ±2 s as the representative "+ frame MIL" rung above — it is the conservative value — and
note that pushing the temporal context to ±5 s buys a further ~+1.8 from the same mechanism.

**Utterance EM is null.** The self-supervised EM loop — reweighting pairs by the model's own
max-region alignment, the direct attempt to climb the *filter* rung without the oracle — does
essentially nothing:

| | −EM | +EM | effect |
|---|---|---|---|
| whole-frame | 52.9 ± 1.7 | 53.6 ± 2.3 | +0.7 |
| region | 62.6 ± 1.7 | 63.8 ± 2.3 | +1.2 |

Both effects sit inside the seed noise (sd ≈ 2). This is a firm version of "the bootstrap does not
ignite": pair-reweighting by the model's own alignment estimate is indistinguishable from zero —
and region MIL has already absorbed most of what it targets.

## The label decomposition

The largest oracle gap is the referent *label* (+18.7 to the 81.3 topline). Holding the pair set
fixed, it splits into three comparable pieces:

![Where the label headroom lives: filtering to referential pairs, selecting the spoken referent
word, and — the largest single piece — supplying the referent when it is *not* spoken at all.
](figures/fig_waterfall_label.png){#fig-label width=80%}

| step | Konkle | Δ | isolates |
|---|---|---|---|
| region-MIL baseline | 62.6 | — | — |
| filtered-natural | 68.5 | +5.9 | which pairs |
| referent word *where spoken* | 73.2 | +4.7 | which word |
| referent word *always* | 81.3 | +8.1 | referent when unspoken (vision) |

The referent is actually spoken in only **~63%** of aligned pairs. Supplying it for the *spoken*
majority (word selection) is worth +4.7; supplying it for the **unspoken 37%** (vision-binding) is
the single largest piece, +8.1, because those pairs otherwise carry no referential signal at all.
This is why @sec-cues aims accessible cues at *identifying the referent* — including visually, when
it isn't said — rather than merely filtering frames.

## Synthesis

The unaided learner reaches **65** — chance-to-65 is bought by pure learning and the two free MIL
selections (region, frame). Everything above, to the **81** ceiling, is an oracle, and the one
self-supervised attempt to climb it (utterance EM) is null. So the bottleneck is not optimization
or scale but **information the learner does not have**: which pairs are referential, and — the
bigger prize — which object is being named, especially when it is never spoken. The next chapter
asks whether the cues children actually use can supply any of it.
